item.title: NASA Stories at the Ion: Building the Moon Base: Challenges and Opportunities at the Lunar South Pole
item.description:
Thursday, July 30, 2026 at 8:30 AM

Location: Ion – Forum Stairs, 4201 Main St., Houston, TX, 77002, United States

Building the Moon Base: Challenges and Opportunities at the Lunar South Pole In this presentation, Moon Base Principal Systems Engineer Shatel Bhakta shares the many challenges NASA must overcome to realize an enduring presence in the lunar South Pole region. He’ll also talk about his journey at NASA, the importance of human space exploration, and what NASA needs from the next generation of aerospace engineers. About the Speaker Shatel Bhakta serves as the principal systems engineer for NASA’s Moon Base. In that role, he takes a system-of-systems view of Moon Base infrastructure, ensuring that all components work together to support NASA’s goal of an enduring human presence in the lunar South Pole region. Prior to working on the Moon Base, Bhakta served as NASA’s lunar architecture lead, guiding a multidisciplinary team across NASA centers to develop a roadmap for crewed exploration of the Moon. This included developing associated conceptual reference missions, concept of operations, site planning guidance, trades and analysis, system element conceptualization, and system-of-systems integration. Bhakta earned his undergraduate degree in mechanical engineering from The University of Texas at Austin and his graduate degree in space architecture from the University of Houston. He is a licensed professional engineer in the state of Texas.  

From Ion District

item.title: Atomistic Spin Simulations and Magneto-Optical Studies of Two-Dimensional van der Waals Magnetic Materials
item.description:
Thursday, July 30, 2026 at 4 PM

Location: Ralph O'Connor Building

  Speaker: Bharadwaj Peela Masters Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Electrical and Computer Engineering Location: Ralph O'Connor Building 300 Two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals magnetic materials provide a unique platform for investigating magnetism at the atomic scale and offer promising opportunities for next-generation spintronic and opto-spintronics technologies. Their weak interlayer bonding, reduced dimensionality, and highly tunable magnetic interactions enable the exploration of both ultrafast nonequilibrium spin dynamics and equilibrium magnetic phase transitions. Understanding these phenomena requires theoretical approaches capable of connecting atomistic magnetic interactions to experimentally observable behavior across multiple timescales. This thesis employs atomistic spin dynamics simulations to investigate magnetic phenomena in chromium-based van der Waals magnets under both dynamic and equilibrium conditions. The simulations are performed within the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert formalism using the VAMPIRE atomistic spin simulation package, enabling the incorporation of exchange interactions, magnetic anisotropy, external magnetic fields, and thermal fluctuations. Together with first-principles-derived magnetic parameters, this framework provides a quantitative description of spin dynamics and thermodynamic magnetic properties. The first part of this work examines ultrafast magnetization dynamics in the van der Waals ferromagnet Cr2Ge2Te6 driven by transient effective magnetic fields generated through chiral-phonon excitation in a neighboring CeF3 substrate. Time-dependent atomistic spin simulations demonstrate that these ultrafast fields induce helicity-dependent magnetization dynamics through rapid domain-wall motion, reproducing experimentally observed demagnetization and recovery processes and providing microscopic insight into chiral-phonon-mediated magnetic proximity effects. The second part of this thesis investigates the magnetic ordering of self-intercalated Cr1+δTe2 compounds. Exchange interactions and magnetic anisotropies obtained from density functional theory calculations are incorporated into atomistic spin simulations to predict equilibrium magnetization and Curie temperatures for different intercalation concentrations. The simulations establish the relationship between Cr intercalation, i competing exchange interactions, and the evolution of magnetic order, demonstrating how first-principles calculations can be combined with atomistic modeling to quantitatively predict finite-temperature magnetic properties. Together, these studies demonstrate the versatility of atomistic spin simulations as a multiscale computational framework for understanding both ultrafast spin dynamics and equilibrium magnetic phase transitions in two-dimensional van der Waals materials. By bridging first-principles calculations, atomistic modeling, and magneto-optical experiments, this work provides fundamental insight into magnetic phenomena across disparate timescales and contributes to the theoretical design of emerging spintronic materials and devices.   (Department : Electrical and Computer Engineering)

From Rice University - Open to the Public

item.title: Symmetry-Resolved Nonlinear Optical Spectroscopy of Twisted Interfaces
item.description:
Thursday, July 30, 2026 at 8 PM

Location: Ralph O'Connor Building

  Speaker: T A M Ragib Shahriar Masters Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Applied Physics Location: Ralph O'Connor Building OES 131 Stacking two crystals with a relative twist creates a moir´e superlattice whose symmetry belongs to neither constituent. In complex oxides this degree of freedom remains largely unexplored and should differ qualitatively from the van der Waals case, since the layers meet through ionic–covalent bonds and can rebond and reconstruct at the junction. The difficulty is that the reconstructed region is a few unit cells thick and buried between two far thicker crystals.   Optical second harmonic generation (SHG) is forbidden in a centrosymmetric bulk within the electric-dipole approximation, so in SrTiO3 (STO) it reports only from surfaces and buried interfaces. Using polarization- and rotation-resolved broadband SHG with nonlinear susceptibility tensor analysis, I first show that the four-fold anisotropy of bare (001) STO arises from the anisotropic bulk electric-quadrupole term rather than the azimuthally isotropic 4mm surface dipole. Modeling a 36◦-twisted STO membrane bilayer as a coherent superposition of surface, bulk-quadrupole, and interfacial sources then yields an interfacial nonlinearity ≈ 0.68 times the STO surface dipole, with a finite imaginary part indicating a near-resonant interfacial electronic structure; first-principles, Raman, and electronmicroscopy results from collaborators attribute it to an asymmetric SrO–TiO2 interface formed on annealing. Because inversion breaking is a weaker condition than chirality, I further developed circular-dichroism SHG and artifact-corrected solid-state circular dichroism, establishing the instrumental floor that any claim of handedness must clear; applied to a twisted STO bicrystal, both are reported as quantitative bounds. I also contributed SHG characterization to studies of fluorinated cubic boron nitride, MoS2 nanoribbon moir´e quantum dots, ferroelectric thin film, and several intermetallic systems. Finally, I propose extending this toolkit from second-harmonic to sum-frequency generation in order to measure the vibrational spectrum of a Wigner crystal—the electron lattice formed when Coulomb repulsion dominates kinetic energy—in transition-metal-dichalcogenide moir´e heterostructures, whose phonons no existing probe resolves directly. This is the subject of my future research, and the apparatus for it has been rebuilt in preparation.https://us04web.zoom.us/j/72834846708?pwd=hDbKa15IbCSlCip9rTGn3bgb0sWk8e.1 (https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://us04web.zoom.us/j/72834846708?pwd=hDbKa15IbCSlCip9rTGn3bgb0sWk8e.1__;!!PcititFMkQu_!r2MdGPs5wJtEVbizlubr45wQ2ekwcqKXEIWH6Zq8Ll1GPUbnRzKkVsj0CckUrlE8zaxjqHW-Tf08-2qH5A$) (Department : Applied Physics)

Broad St. in the heart of downtown Columbus. Built in 1926, this stunning theater is one of the most beautiful performance spaces in Ohio, featuring ornate architecture, a grand lobby, and exceptional acoustics. item.title: Houston Restaurant Weeks 2026
item.description:
Saturday, August 1, 2026 at 12 AM

Houston Restaurant Weeks is the largest annual fundraiser for America’s largest food bank, the Houston Food Bank. It’s a month-long dining extravaganza featuring specially priced lunches, brunches, and dinners at restaurants from The Woodlands to Galveston. Participating restaurants make donations based on how many prix fixe brunches, lunches, and dinners they sell during the event. Diners are not solicited for donations. Beginning July 15, diners can visit HoustonRestaurantWeeks.com to view the 2026 list of restaurants that have committed to participate, along with their HRW menus. The event includes restaurants located in Harris, Galveston, and Montgomery counties. The Galveston County Food Bank and Montgomery County Food Bank are part of the Houston Food Bank’s Affiliate Food Banks. The Houston Food Bank provides food to these smaller food banks, which in turn distribute the food to hunger relief charities in a portion of HFB’s service area. The Houston Food Bank certifies that their Affiliate Food Banks meet Feeding America standards.

item.title: Houston Comic Exchange II
item.description:
Saturday, August 1, 2026 at 10 AM

Houston Comic Exchange II – Built for Comic Collectors Summer is prime comic-hunting season, and CCS Houston Comic Exchange II brings together collectors, dealers, and fans for a day of buying, selling, trading, and discovering comics. From key issues and first appearances to hidden gems and box-fresh finds, every table offers something worth digging for. No gatekeeping, no pressure, just comics and the people who love them.   📅 Saturday, August 1, 2026 | 10AM – 5PM 📍 9700 Bissonnet St, Unit 1500, Houston, TX 🎟️ FREE Entry + FREE Parking   🔥 Event Highlights 🔥 📦 50 Vendor Tables – All Comics, All Formats Singles, back issues, key issues, first appearances, graded slabs, raw runs, indie and small press, variant covers. Vendor tables dedicated entirely to comics, no toys, no filler. If you’re a comic collector, this floor was built for you.   🔍 Key Issues and First Appearances This is where the hunt lives. Vendors bring the deep cuts, raw back issues worth digging through, graded books if you’re chasing condition, and the kind of keys that actually show up when serious collectors are clearing their own collections to make room.   📚 Back-Issue Digging and Indie Discovery Not every great find is a grail. Long boxes of back issues across decades and publishers, plus indie comics and small press titles that never make it to a standard shop shelf. Come with a list or come ready to browse – both work.   🤝 Vendors Who Collect Too The people behind these tables are the same people who will ask what you’re hunting before they start pulling books for you. The Houston Comic Exchange is a community floor first. The conversations are part of the event.   🛒 Vendor Table Applications Houston comic vendors: we’re gathering a focused comics-only crowd, and free entry is driving serious foot traffic. Apply for your table here 👉🏻 https://forms.gle/7q6pjcoiJTPbJouP8   The key issue you’ve been tracking is probably in one of those long boxes this summer. The Houston Comic Exchange II, August 1. Free entry, free parking, always.

From CCS Houston

Official TicketsResale Tickets About the Performer Josh Johnson is a rising star in the stand-up comedy world, best known for his sharp wit, absurdist observations, and uniquely cerebral comedic style. He has appeared on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon, The Daily Show, and his own Netflix special, earning him a devoted fanbase across the country. Johnson’s comedy blends intellectual humor with relatable everyday experiences, often exploring the quirks of modern life, social dynamics, and the human condition — all delivered with impeccable timing and a laid-back confidence that keeps audiences laughing from start to finish. His Comedy Band Camp concept is a unique live experience that combines stand-up performance with a musical, camp-style atmosphere — making it one of the most talked-about touring shows of 2026. Event Details Date: Saturday, August 1, 2026 Show Time: 5:00 PM (Early Show) Venue: Taft Theatre, 317 East 5th Street, Cincinnati, OH 45202 Doors Open: Approximately 4:00 PM Age Restrictions: All ages welcome; some content may be intended for mature audiences Note: A second show (Late Show) is also available at 8:30 PM on the same date About the Venue The Taft Theatre is one of Cincinnati’s most beloved and historic entertainment venues, located in the heart of downtown at 317 East 5th Street. Built in 1928, the Taft Theatre is a stunning example of Art Deco architecture and has hosted some of the biggest names in comedy, music, and the performing arts for nearly a century. With a seating capacity of approximately 2,500, the Taft offers an intimate yet grand atmosphere that makes every seat feel close to the action. The venue features excellent sightlines, superior acoustics, and a warm, classic ambiance that enhances any live performance experience. Amenities include a full-service bar, concessions, and accessible seating options. Parking is available in several nearby garages and surface lots throughout downtown Cincinnati. The venue is also conveniently accessible via public transit. What to Expect Josh Johnson’s Comedy Band Camp is not your average stand-up show. This unique live experience brings together comedy, music, and an immersive camp-style atmosphere that has been wowing audiences on tour across the country. Expect a high-energy evening filled with Josh Johnson’s signature brand of smart, observational humor, along with special musical elements that make this show a one-of-a-kind event. Whether you’re a longtime fan or discovering Josh Johnson for the first time, this show promises to be an unforgettable night of laughter and entertainment. The Early Show at 5:00 PM is perfect for those who want to enjoy the full experience and still have the rest of the evening free. Arrive early to grab a drink, find your seat, and soak in the incredible atmosphere of the historic Taft Theatre. item.title: Houston Toy Exchange III
item.description:
Sunday, August 2, 2026 at 10 AM

Houston Toy Exchange III — The Floor Is Loaded, Houston Somewhere on this floor is the piece you have been hunting for months. 🔥 Houston Toy Exchange III is a pure toy marketplace, no convention noise, no filler. Just collectors, families, and dealers moving action figures, vintage finds, and modern grails across one packed floor at CCS Houston. The fun is in the hunt: digging through a bin you have never seen, talking shop with someone who knows the line better than you do, and walking out with something you did not expect to find.   📅 Date: Sunday, August 2, 2026 | 10AM – 5PM 📍 Location: 9700 Bissonnet St, #1500, Houston, TX 77036 🎟️ FREE Entry + FREE Parking   🔥 What You’ll Find on the Floor 🔥 🛍️ Toy Marketplace Tables packed with action figures, vintage toys, sealed and loose, nostalgia pieces, and the modern lines collectors are actually chasing right now. Every table is its own dig. Come search the floor.   💰 Buy, Sell, Trade Bring the toys you are ready to pass along or trade up for something you have been chasing. Collectors and vendors are buying, selling, and trading all day. Connect, negotiate, and keep great pieces moving through the community.   🔍 Toy Appraisals Holding something and not sure what it’s worth? One of our experienced vendors is running toy appraisals all day, sharing insights on value, rarity, and trade potential so you can make confident, informed deals on the floor.   🧩 Toy Scavenger Hunt Challenge Turn the hunt into a game. Work the marketplace and complete the Toy Hunt Challenge by tracking down specific toy categories across multiple booths for a shot at prizes and collector bragging rights.   📸 Toy Flex Wall Score something special? Show it off. Snap a photo of your best pickup at the Toy Flex Wall and share your find with the community.   Longtime collector or just starting out, Houston Toy Exchange III is about connecting, swapping stories, and keeping the love of toys alive together. Bring your toys, bring your curiosity, pull up.   Want in as a vendor? Tables are open: https://tinyurl.com/CCSGuestVendorFromHouston   Houston Toy Exchange III. Bring your toys, bring your curiosity, and come move some pieces.

From CCS Houston

item.title: Influencer–Brand Partnerships: A Matching Approach
item.description:
Monday, August 3, 2026 at 8 PM

Location: Kraft Hall

  Speaker: Masoud Jabbari Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Economics Location: Kraft Hall 102 This thesis studies how brands allocate advertising budgets across bundles of Instagram influencers in a centralized platform, addressing the business problem of platform assignment potentially overriding brand preferences. I develop a structural matching model to recover preferences over influencer scale, engagement, and thematic focus, estimated conditional on campaign characteristics using administrative platform data. Preferences are identified using pairwise stability, first in matches alone and then jointly in matches and prices, leveraging influencer posted prices and a control-function approach based on hedonic regressions to address price endogeneity and persistent unobserved quality. The estimates indicate that follower count is most valuable for follower-growth campaigns, whereas engagement and thematic concentration become relatively more important for sales- and lead-generation objectives. Counterfactual analyses highlight the important role of Nano and Micro influencers in maintaining brand utility and demonstrate that platform assignments in CPM campaigns can be substantially improved when aligned with estimated preferences. Methodologically, this thesis demonstrates how preferences can be recovered in platform-mediated matching environments with limited choice-set observability, providing a tractable framework for analyzing digital advertising markets and informing more effective platform allocation design.   (Department : Economics)

From Rice University - Open to the Public

This year, the goats will be working on a 7 acre area in the northwest corner of the Arboretum between the 610 Parking Loop, the Ravine Trail, and the Event Lawn. Read below for some helpful tips for viewing the goats at work! Are you an Arboretum Member? If so, join us on Friday, August 7 from 10:00 am – 12:00 pm for a fun, free Members-only Meet the Mowers event! 2026 Goat visit map Goat Viewing Tips Park at either entrance and follow the yellow arrows along the trails directing you from the Nature Center to the goats’ current location. You can also look at the Goat Visit Map to plan your walk. Stay on sidewalks and trails. Keep children and dogs away from the fence – it is electrified to keep predators like coyotes out of the area. Do not try to feed or pet the goats. They are helping us clear species like poison ivy, and the oils can get on your skin. Take lots of photos – if you post them on social media, tag @houstonarboretum so we can see them!

item.title: Signal or Noise: Can Team Neurodynamics Add to the Understanding of Teamwork Beyond Self-Report and Observation?
item.description:
Tuesday, August 4, 2026 at 3 PM

Location: Sewall Hall

  Speaker: Maha Khalid Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Psychology Location: Sewall Hall 250 Progress in understanding teamwork depends on progress in measuring it. Traditional approaches to assessing teamwork, such as self-report and observational measures, provide valuable insight into team functioning. However, many existing approaches capture static or retrospective accounts of teamwork and may not fully reflect how teamwork evolves moment-to-moment. As a result, there is growing interest in methods capable of continuously capturing team dynamics, particularly in action teams, which are characterized by time pressure, high stakes, and rapidly changing task demands. One such approach, team neurodynamics, uses electroencephalography (EEG) to quantify patterns of neurophysiological organization across team members during a task. Although team neurodynamics has shown promise as a continuous measure of team functioning, its value beyond established measures remains unclear. The present study examined the incremental validity of team neurodynamics, using the EEG-derived Neurodynamic Information (NI) measure, in predicting objective mission performance beyond traditional self-report and observational measures. Twenty four-person teams recruited from Rice University's undergraduate and graduate student population participated in a simulated military task developed in Unity to mimic a Marine Fire Support Team (FiST) mission. Teamwork was assessed using a condensed Team Diagnostic Survey, an event-based observational coding framework, and team neurodynamics. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses evaluated the incremental validity of these measures. Predictors were entered sequentially from least resource-intensive to most: self-report, observation, and team neurodynamics. The predictive utility of teamwork measures differed across the two experimental missions. During the more challenging mission, self-report explained approximately 46% of the variance in objective mission performance, and observation explained an additional 13% of the variance, whereas no significant predictors emerged during the less demanding mission. The team neurodynamic measure did not significantly predict objective mission performance in either mission and did not explain additional variance beyond the traditional teamwork measures. However, in the more challenging mission, exploratory mediation analyses indicated that maximum NI, representing the team's greatest degree of neurodynamic organization, demonstrated a statistically significant indirect relationship with objective mission performance through self-report. These findings support the utility of self-report and observational measures for predicting objective mission performance under more demanding task conditions while providing preliminary evidence suggesting that periods of peak neurodynamic organization may be associated with teams' subjective evaluations of their functioning. The exploratory mediation findings build on the Interactive Team Cognition perspective, suggesting that peak neurodynamic organization may be associated with the interactional processes through which teams coordinate their activities and subsequently evaluate their functioning. This work contributes to understanding the complementary role of neurodynamic indicators alongside established self-report and observational approaches.   (Department : Psychology)

From Rice University - Open to the Public

item.title: Characterizing the role of Nephronectin during Anterior Eye Development in Mice
item.description:
Wednesday, August 5, 2026 at 7 PM

Location: Keck Hall

  Speaker: Matthew Robert Garis Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: BioSciences-Biochemistry and Cell Biology Location: Keck Hall 102 Anterior eye development is a complex process involving the migration, proliferation, patterning and interactions between many difference cell types in order to achieve the niche tissue properties required for proper sight. The periocular mesenchyme interacts with nascent ocular tissues and extracellular matrix proteins to provide a transparent cornea. While support structures like sensory nerves and anterior eye vasculature are formed and patterned with tight spatiotemporal regulation to sustain ocular structures. Cellular interactions with the extracellular matrix are essential in regulating these morphogenic processes, but which specific component proteins achieve these effects and the signaling pathways involved are not well understood. These studies were developed to further understand the role of the extracellular matrix protein nephronectin (Npnt) during anterior eye development. While the protein has been researched during avian cornea development, its role in mice was yet to be described. The method by which these two organisms develop the cornea varies greatly and this opened the potential to discover species-specific functions of Npnt. To this end, I utilized a Npnt mutant mouse model to probe how the murine cornea is formed without this matrix protein. I show that Npnt is utilized as a migration substrate by the periocular mesenchyme (POM), as its absence leads to a reduction in corneal thickness and decreased cell counts but does not affect proliferation capacity. This result was confirmed via in vitro POM explant experiments demonstrating the ability for these cells to use Npnt as a substrate to migrate upon and blocking the EGFR pathway abolished that capacity. Thus, I found Npnt to mediate the migration of POM cells into the murine cornea during development by activation of the EGFR pathway. Npnt has been shown to play a role in angiogenesis and sensory nerve patterning during development but the protein's involvement in these processes during anterior eye development has never been investigated. I show that Npnt has the correct spatiotemporal expression to potentially influence the migration and patterning of the vasculature and nerves that project to the anterior eye. Utilizing whole mount immunohistochemistry experiments, I found that Npnt is needed for the proper patterning of the choroid vasculature and for the proper projection profile of sensory nerve innervation into the anterior eye. I furthered these results using primary neuron cell culture experiments of dissociated trigeminal ganglia from embryonic mice, discovering that Npnt attenuates migration of sensory nerves in an integrin dependent manner. Finally, I definitively determined the developmental stage at which the corneal endothelial basement membrane, the Descemet's membrane (DM), is first formed with transmission electron microscopy. Npnt is expressed by the endothelial cells during development and is integrated into the membrane with changing spatial expression relative to other major basement membrane components. I found that Npnt is expressed not only during development of the membrane but is sustained throughout the life of an organism, suggesting it may be involved in the maintenance of the corneal endothelium or in the Descemet's membrane barrier functions. Overall, in this thesis, I identified a species-specific mechanism for how the extracellular matrix protein Npnt facilitates POM migration into the developing cornea. I expanded upon this by finding Npnt is a substrate for endothelial vasculature and sensory nerves during anterior eye formation. Identifying these functional roles for Npnt during development and noting its continued expression in the Descemet's membrane provides the basis for Npnt and its receptors being potential targets for corneal cell-matrix therapies.   Matthew Garis is inviting you to a scheduled Zoom meeting. item.title: Advancing Genetic Code Expansion: From Genome-Wide Host Reprogramming to Innovative Biological Applications
item.description:
Thursday, August 6, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: BioScience Research Collaborative

  Speaker: Mengxi Zhang Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Chemistry Location: BioScience Research Collaborative 282 Genetic code expansion (GCE) enables noncanonical amino acids (ncAAs) with diverse chemical and physical properties to be introduced into proteins at defined positions. This technology has provided valuable tools for protein labeling, functional regulation, biomolecular engineering and the investigation of biological processes. Despite the rapid development of GCE, many genetically encoded ncAAs have been demonstrated primarily at the level of protein incorporation, while their potential for solving broader biological and engineering problems remains underexplored. In addition, the production of ncAA-containing proteins is often limited by inefficient stop-codon suppression and by the cellular environment in which the orthogonal translation system operates. In this dissertation, we expand the applications of genetically encoded ncAAs in material engineering and live-cell imaging and investigate endogenous host factors that regulate ncAA-containing protein production. To introduce material-binding properties into proteins and living cells, 3,4-dihydroxy-L-phenylalanine (DOPA), a catechol-containing amino acid found in mussel adhesive proteins, was genetically incorporated into proteins at defined positions. Optimization of the DOPA incorporation system enabled the production of homogeneous DOPA-containing proteins with enhanced binding to a broad range of organic and inorganic materials. The material-binding capability of DOPA was further combined with intrinsically disordered proteins to generate adhesive antifouling proteins. Extending this strategy from proteins to living cells, DOPA was incorporated into a bacterial surface protein to substantially enhance bacterial attachment to different materials. The improved interaction between engineered bacteria and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) also facilitated bacterial degradation of PET, demonstrating the application of GCE in protein, material and cellular engineering. In addition to creating new protein functions, genetically encoded ncAAs can serve as compact probes for studying dynamic biological processes. A series of rotor-based fluorescent ncAAs was developed to monitor local protein microenvironment changes in living cells. Among these amino acids, AnapTh displayed strong responses to environmental polarity and viscosity. Computational redesign of an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase enabled the site-specific incorporation of AnapTh into proteins in mammalian cells. Placement of AnapTh at selected residues allowed real-time monitoring of local environmental changes during the aggregation of human superoxide dismutase and Huntingtin proteins and during the clustering of STIM1 and CRY2. Distinct fluorescence responses observed at different incorporation sites revealed spatially resolved changes within individual protein regions, providing a method to visualize protein aggregation, clustering and their reverse processes with high spatial precision. While these studies demonstrate the functional potential of genetically encoded ncAAs, their broader utility depends on efficient and faithful ncAA-containing protein production. To investigate how the host cell contributes to this process, a genome-wide screen of the Escherichia coli Keio single-gene knockout collection was performed using a dual-fluorescent amber-suppression reporter. Nine gene deletions reproducibly altered reporter production across different ncAA incorporation systems, indicating that GCE is regulated by diverse endogenous cellular processes. Among these candidates, rplI, which encodes the 50S ribosomal protein bL9, was further investigated. Deletion of rplI reduced overall protein expression, increased relative amber-codon readthrough and decreased the translation elongation rate, linking ribosome dynamics to ncAA incorporation. Sequence Display was subsequently used to examine the sequence-function landscape of RplI and identified its C-terminal region as an informative target for further engineering. Together, this dissertation develops and explores important applications of genetically encoded ncAAs while providing insights into the host translational mechanisms that govern their incorporation.   (Department : Chemistry)

item.title: Quantifying Many-Body Contextuality with Multiplayer Nonlocal Games from Stabilizer Codes
item.description:
Thursday, August 6, 2026 at 7 PM

Location: Space Science Building

  Speaker: Wanbing Zhao Masters Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Physics & Astronomy Location: Space Science Building 301A Quantum contextuality is a fundamental property of quantum mechanics that captures the impossibility of reproducing quantum measurement outcomes from pre-existing classical values. Contextuality in few-particle quantum systems is commonly studied using Bell inequalities, but its emergence in large-scale, many-particle quantum systems remains poorly understood. Such many-body contextuality has attracted renewed attention in quantum information science through its formulation in terms of "nonlocal games" played with stabilizer codes, which are mathematically equivalent to Bell inequalities. However, work in this field has largely focused on determining whether such nonlocal games exhibit quantum advantage. To quantify many-body contextuality, we develop a systematic theory of nonlocal games defined on n-qubit stabilizer codes via nonlinear Boolean functions. The theory yields a universal upper bound of 7/8 on the classical value of such games that admit quantum advantage. For cyclic cluster states and toric codes, we prove that the classical values of the associated games approach 1/2 exponentially fast in n, resulting in exponentially large Bell-inequality violations. Going beyond these lattice examples, we show that exponential Bell-inequality violations are generic among random graph states, occurring with high probability over Erdős–Rényi ensembles with fixed edge probability p \in (0,1). These results provide a scalable path toward testing quantum contextuality on current and future quantum devices.   (Department : Physics & Astronomy)

item.title: Houston TCG Con X
item.description:
Friday, August 7, 2026 at 10 AM

💥 Houston… Round X: From one to ten – What a pull it’s been! 🎉 🎴 Three Days • FREE Entry • 100+ Vendors • Nonstop Trades! What started as a small weekend card show has turned into a full-on collector movement. Houston TCG Con is back at CCS with Round X: a full 3-day weekend built on trades, collecting, and community. More time to dig. More time to trade. More time to find something you didn’t even know you needed. 🃏🤝   📅 Date: August 7-9, 2026 ⏰ Time: Friday: 3PM – 10PM | Saturday: 10AM – 6PM | Sunday: 10AM – 5PM 📍 Location: 9700 Bissonnet St, #1500, Houston, TX 77036 🎟️ FREE Entry + FREE Parking!   🔥 Event Highlights 🔥 🃏 100+ TCG Vendors — The Houston Trade Floor Shop from 100+ curated vendors from across Texas and beyond. Tables will be stacked with: ✅ Top titles including Pokémon, Magic: The Gathering, Yu-Gi-Oh!, One Piece, Lorcana, Digimon, Weiss Schwarz, and more. ✅ Sealed product + booster boxes ✅ Graded slabs + collector singles ✅ Binder deals + playable staples ✅ Japanese imports + hard-to-find pickups ✅ Sleeves, top loaders, storage & accessories   ⚡ Buy • Sell • Trade — All Weekend This is what Houston TCG Con is known for. Bring your binders, make the deals you’ve been waiting for, and connect with collectors. This is where grails change hands and collections level up.   🔍 On-Site Grading Submissions & Card Restorations — Cappy’s Cards! Have a card you’ve been thinking about grading? Or one that needs a little restoration? Cappy’s Cards will be on-site helping collectors with grading submissions, restoration services, and expert insight all weekend.   🤝 Built by the Community — 10 Rounds Strong From first packs opened around the kitchen table to the cards you still chase today, this is where it all comes back. The trades, the stories, the people you meet along the way, Round X is a milestone for everyone who grew up with the hobby and never really left it. item.title: Thalamo-cortical evoked effective connectivity to guide personalized neuromodulation in epilepsy
item.description:
Friday, August 7, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: BioScience Research Collaborative

  Speaker: Jasper Wang Masters Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Electrical and Computer Engineering Location: BioScience Research Collaborative 875 Thalamic deep brain stimulation (DBS) has emerged as a promising treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy. Besides the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT), the only FDA-approved target, the centromedian nucleus (CM) and pulvinar have also been shown to be promising targets. However, outcomes vary both across and within stimulation targets, and to date there is no consensus on the optimal stimulation site within each thalamic nucleus. Here, we hypothesized that effective connectivity, as quantified by thalamo-cortical evoked potentials (TCEPs), could guide personalized DBS target selection. We recorded scalp EEG responses to single-pulse electrical stimulation delivered via thalamic DBS electrodes in 15 epilepsy patients. Voxel-based linear mixed-effects modeling was applied to TCEP data to generate stimulation-response maps with high spatiotemporal resolution. We provided group-level TCEP stimulation-response maps of the CM and pulvinar, and showed that pulvinar and CM subregions selectively engage distinct cortical networks, detectable with non-invasive scalp EEG. The pulvinar showed a medial-to-lateral gradient: medial pulvinar mapped to anterior temporal cortex, middle pulvinar to mid-temporal cortex, and lateral pulvinar to parietal and posterior temporal cortex. Lateral-dorsal CM showed strong connectivity to frontocentral regions. Finally, we demonstrated a significant correlation between acute TCEP response and long-term seizure reduction rate within the same patient cohort, supporting the clinical translational potential of this approach.   Zoom link: https://www.google.com/url?q=https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/j/93695667394?pwd%3DBlRXICqUVKI2MZvD1W2ySZwFarWfq1.1&sa=D&source=calendar&ust=1785182094516539&usg=AOvVaw321gy5b1gZlvJrgy-BIX9J (Department : Electrical and Computer Engineering)

item.title: First Fridays Presents Tina Cardona
item.description:
Friday, August 7, 2026 at 7:30 PM

Location: Inprint House, 1520 W Main St, Houston, TX, 77006, United States

Free and open to the public Doors @ 7 pm Pop-up poet @ 7:30 pm Featured poet @ 7:40 pm Open mic @ 8:15 pm Inprint is proud to serve as the host for the First Fridays Reading Series. The First Fridays Reading Series is the oldest poetry series in Houston and was organized by Robert Clark from 1975-2019. Today, First Fridays events are curated and hosted by local community members. The August featured reader will be Tina Cardona, a community maker for Houston poets as a co-founder of hotpoet.org. She is a psychotherapist, yoga teacher, earth advocate, dog guardian, soothsayer, mother and partner, and is also in a long-standing, conflictual relationship with poetry. You can find her wandering at dawn and at dusk muttering with trees. The opening pop-up poet will be Michael J. Galko, a retired scientist and active poet from Houston. He is the artist responsible for ‘haiku house’, a residential art installation consisting of hundreds of original wood-burned and painted haiku. He was a finalist in the 2020 Naugatuck River Review and the 2022 Bellevue Literary Review poetry contests. Recent poems appear in Spillway Magazine, Atlanta Review, Silk Road Review, and Plainsongs, among other journals. For more information about the First Fridays Reading Series, click here. To join the First Fridays Facebook group, click here.

Baldwin laid out Westmoreland Place in 1902, its location on the southwestern side of what is now Midtown was considered the very edge of Houston. item.title: Intoxication in British Literature, 1660-1760
item.description:
Monday, August 10, 2026 at 4 PM

  Speaker: Rowan Morar Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: English "Intoxication in British Literature, 1660-1760" argues for reading literary representations of intoxicants and altered states of mind, as a normative condition of Enlightenment life and a feature of literary representation itself. Drawing from social history, I trace how mass markets for drugs, such as plantation produced tobacco and spirits, as well as opium left their imprints on the works of key authors of British literary history—Lord Rochester, Aphra Behn, Daniel Defoe, and Charlotte Lennox. I argue that these writers from 1660-1760, the Restoration to the mid-Enlightenment period, represented the influx of colonially produced drugs that became fiscal necessities for statecraft in order to make tacit assumptions about everyday self-regulation, socialization, and politics visible. Profane appetites were as fundamentally changed in Britain as they were central to concepts of subjectivity in the violent colonial theaters producing the intoxicants for an era of taste and refinement. The construction of a subjective experience of intoxication in poems, the performance of drunkenness on the stage, the narrative accounts of inner consciousness affected by rum or tobacco, wine or opium—all offer means for seeing double: the work of intoxicants on literature and literary intoxication during an increasingly global era of mass intoxication.   https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/s/92686072682 (Department : English)

From Rice University - Open to the Public

Event details

item.title: An Apparatus for Quantum Simulation with Rydberg Atoms
item.description:
Monday, August 10, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: Brockman Hall for Physics

  Speaker: Brent Kruzel Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Physics & Astronomy Location: Brockman Hall for Physics 300 This thesis presents the design, construction, and characterization of a new experimental platform for quantum simulation using ultracold strontium-88 Rydberg atoms. The apparatus was developed to support future optical-tweezer based experiments that realize synthetic dimensions through coherent millimeter-wave coupling between neighboring Rydberg states while providing the optical access, electric- and magnetic-field control, and state-sensitive detection required for precision measurements. A new science chamber was designed and integrated with laser cooling, selective field ionization, and charged-particle detection systems, while electromagnetic simulations were used to optimize millimeter-wave delivery and field uniformity. Experimental characterization of the completed apparatus includes measurements of static electric-field compensation, millimeter-wave polarization purity, and coherent Rydberg spectroscopy through Rabi and Ramsey techniques. In addition, analysis methods were developed to extract relative Rydberg-state populations from selective field ionization signals, and new high-precision microwave spectroscopy measurements were incorporated into an updated determination of the quantum defect Rydberg-Ritz parameters for the singlet S, P, and D Rydberg series of strontium. Together, these developments establish the experimental and analytical foundation for future quantum simulation experiments on this new apparatus.   (Department : Physics & Astronomy)

From Rice University - Open to the Public

item.title: Essays on the Energy Transition in Electricity Markets
item.description:
Wednesday, August 12, 2026 at 9 PM

Location: Baker Hall

Renewable energy is restructuring the generation mix in electricity markets, simultaneously driving thermal retirement, substantially suppressing wholesale energy prices when and where they are generating, and redirecting investment toward new technologies such as battery storage to compensate for their effects. This dissertation studies all three channels in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) market. Each chapter takes a different angle and methodology: structural estimation of retirement decisions, analytical equilibrium theory for renewable dynamics, and reduced-form spatial analysis of investment composition. The first chapter estimates a dynamic discrete choice model of retirement for natural gas and coal-fired generators in ERCOT, treating exit as an irreversible optimal stopping problem under forward-looking expectations. All 45 observed exits in the estimation panel occur at strictly positive operating profit, consistent with retirement as a forward-looking continuation-value decision rather than a current-period margin trigger. The retirement decision in the model has two channels: a current-period flow payoff in which operating profit and age enter directly, and a forward-looking continuation value that summarizes the expected path of future operating profit. Operating profit is constructed at unit resolution from a 15-minute spark-spread payoff that combines real-time nodal locational marginal prices (LMPs) and fuel-cost indices (Henry Hub for gas units, delivered coal costs for coal units). Ancillary service revenue recovered from the ERCOT 60-Day Security-Constrained Economic Dispatch (SCED) record is added, and pro-rated fixed operating and maintenance costs are subtracted. Operating profit enters the flow payoff positively and significantly (coefficient +0.653, t-statistic 3.15 under a random-effects specification). Generator age enters negatively (-0.510), marginal under random effects and strongly significant without them. Wind and solar shape retirement decisions through the operating-profit transition kernel rather than the flow payoff. Their persistence in the kernel transmits into continuation values, which is how the model captures the effect of renewable trajectories on exit. Both kernel coefficients are negative (wind -0.157, solar -0.030), reflecting the merit-order erosion of incumbent operating profit, with wind the stronger channel and solar the weaker. Two counterfactual exercises explore the implications of the estimated structural model. A wind-versus-solar dose-response varies zonal renewable shares and shows how marginal renewable expansion reshapes the composition of the surviving fleet. A forward projection built from the April 2026 ERCOT Generator Interconnection Status report calibrates expected renewable buildout. Through 2035, the fleet's existing age distribution dominates retirement, while the renewable buildout contributes only marginally. The structural estimates and counterfactuals provide a reference point for policymakers and market planners assessing how the dispatchable thermal fleet evolves under continued renewable buildout in ERCOT. The second chapter extends the analytical framework of Green and Leautier (2015) in two directions. First, we derive a complete set of marginal impact results under a Feed-in Premium (FiP), an extension they identified as an open problem. Under FiP, renewable producers receive the wholesale price plus a fixed premium per MWh and curtail output when the price falls below the negative of the premium. The results cover the long-run generation mix, the per-MW market value of renewables, the equilibrium tax, and the required marginal subsidy. Because renewables avoid producing in the worst-priced states, the per-MW market value of renewable capacity falls more slowly as renewable penetration grows under FiP than under a fixed-price Feed-in Tariff. Second, we adapt the framework to the ERCOT market, which uses an Operating Reserve Demand Curve (ORDC) to set scarcity prices in lieu of a forward capacity market. ERCOT's ORDC applies a scarcity adder to the real-time energy price when operating reserves are low, calibrated to the expected cost of the curtailment those reserves would prevent. Throughout the chapter's sample period (2019-2023), the ORDC operated as an ex post adder to the energy clearing price under sequential energy and ancillary service auctions, rather than as a co-optimized shadow value within a single security-constrained dispatch. We adopt the economic logic of Hogan (2013), who derived the ORDC for a co-optimized setting, and adapt it to this pre-co-optimization institutional environment. The principal theoretical result is that the ORDC does not directly affect the rate at which renewable per-MW values fall with renewable penetration. Where infra-marginal conventional generators are at capacity, marginal changes in reserves shift rents to those generators without altering the rate at which renewable value declines. The ORDC's effect on renewable values therefore operates indirectly, through the equilibrium generation mix. A calibration exercise using ERCOT data confirms three qualitative findings. The FiP reduces the per-MW subsidy needed to sustain renewable entry and slows the rate at which the per-MW value of renewables falls. Nuclear capacity exits the equilibrium at approximately 80 GW of wind under FiT and at approximately 77 GW under ERCOT's ORDC-based market structure, while the FiP retains nuclear across the full simulated range. The earlier exit reflects a demand-channel asymmetry that the chapter establishes analytically and the calibration confirms. The combined FiP-ERCOT case is the policy-relevant one for ERCOT, since the federal Production Tax Credit shares the FiP's premium-on-top-of-price structure. Under this regime, the calibration shows substantially slower per-MW value decline than without the FiP, with nuclear retention preventing the abrupt acceleration that follows nuclear exit. This analysis bridges the analytical framework of Green and Leautier (2015) with the scarcity-pricing logic of Hogan (2013), and the ERCOT calibration provides its empirical interpretation. The third chapter estimates a discrete choice model of generator investment across ERCOT's four load zones over 2011-2024. Developers choose among five technologies (wind, solar, combined-cycle gas, open-cycle gas, and battery storage), grouped into dispatchable and non-dispatchable segments. Entry composition is estimated with a multinomial logit in the Berry (1994) log-odds inversion, with operating profit instrumented by national fuel-cost shifters and rival characteristics. Fixed cost deters entry (-3.63, p < 0.001) and federal subsidies shift composition toward the subsidized technologies (+2.29, p < 0.001). Both results are stable when year and zone fixed effects are added and when the model is re-estimated as a Poisson count model, which retains the zone-years with no entry that the log-odds inversion must drop. Entry shows no detectable response to annual energy margins. Gas-fired entry falls well below what observed payoffs alone would predict. The results quantify the mapping from ERCOT's price signals to the technology composition of investment and inform the resource adequacy debate.

item.title: Jesus Benavente: NUESTROWORLD
item.description:
Thursday, August 13, 2026 at 12 AM

Location: DiverseWorks, @ 5601 B Navigation Blvd & Various Locations, 5601 B Navigation Blvd, Houston, TX, 77011, United States

Opening Thursday, August 13, 2026 | 6 – 8 PM Gallery Hours: Thurs – Sat 12 – 6 PM NUESTROWORLD is a satirical solo exhibition by Brooklyn-based artist Jesus Benavente, conceived of as a visual album and immersive “amusement park.” This project features interconnected works unfolding across the gallery and city, collectively highlighting Houston’s cyclical history of ambition, folly, and heartbreak. The title NUESTROWORLD is a play on Astroworld and uses Spanglish to create the phrase “The World Is Ours.” The project draws inspiration from popular events that mark specific eras of Houston’s history, such as the opening of the world-famous Astrodome and Astroworld Park in the late 60’s, Selena’s iconic Rodeo performances in the 90’s, and the folklore surrounding the 1836 capture of Santa Anna during the Battle of San Jacinto as part of the Texas Revolution. Together, they build a story, a world developed over time that underscores sacrifice, instills resilience, and highlights a Texas attitude of “come and take it.”  ARTIST BIO: Jesus Benavente is a visual artist based in Brooklyn, New York. Jesus earned an MFA from Rutgers University and attended Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture. Recent exhibitions and performances include the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York; Queens Museum, Queens; LTD Los Angeles, Los Angeles; Performa 13, New York; Acre Projects, Chicago; Chinati Foundation, Marfa; the Neuberger Museum of Art, Purchase, NY; Shin Museum of Art, South Korea; Vox Populi, Philadelphia; Socrates Sculpture Park, New York; and Austin Museum of Art. Benavente was born in San Antonio, Texas.

item.title: Illuminating the dynamics of magmatic systems: from bubbles to the lithosphere, from a computer to the lab
item.description:
Thursday, August 13, 2026 at 7 PM

Location: Keith-Wiess Geological Laboratories

  Speaker: Gaetano Ferrante Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences Location: Keith-Wiess Geological Laboratories KWGL 123 Volcanoes are the surface manifestation of Earth's great geodynamic forces. They provide an invaluable window into geologic processes that are hidden from direct observation, yet they represent a significant hazard for millions of people around the world. Investigating the dynamics of volcanic systems is thus crucial to better understand our planet and improve assessments of volcanic hazard. Volcanic processes occur over a wide range of spatial and temporal scales, motivating the use of correspondingly diverse methodologies to investigate their dynamics. In this thesis, I will employ experiments, numerical modeling and data analysis to address some of the most fundamental, yet widely disputed, questions in volcanology. One of the major controls on the eruptive style and ensuing hazard of a volcano is the viscosity of its magma. Among other factors, gas bubbles suspended in the magma can either increase or decrease its viscosity, strongly influencing eruptive dynamics. In Chapter 1, I will present results from rheology experiments conducted on natural pumice samples to understand how bubbles affect the viscosity of magma. I will propose a new and unambiguous constitutive equation for the viscosity of bubbly magmas that can be used to better model volcanic eruptions and lava flows. Magmatic systems can extend for tens of kilometers from the asthenosphere, where magma is produced, to the Earth's surface, where it is eventually erupted. Whether volcanoes are controlled from the bottom-up or from the top-down is still a major question in volcanology. In Chapter 2, I will couple a numerical model of magma flow at the lithospheric scale with surface-available observations collected during the past 30 years at Kīlauea volcano (Hawaiʻi), to shed light on the dynamics of its magmatic supply pathway. "Why do eruptions end?" is a fundamental, yet overlooked question in volcanology. In 2018, Kīlauea experienced its largest eruption in more than 200 years of history, providing an unprecedented set of observations that helped volcanologists improve our understanding of caldera-forming eruptions. More than 8 years after the start of the eruption, the reasons underlying its sudden and unexpected conclusion still remain, for the most part, a mystery. In Chapter 3, I will jointly analyze a diverse set of geophysical data collected during Kīlauea's 2018 eruption to shed light on its progression and enigmatic end, providing a framework to interpret the evolution of past and future caldera-forming eruptions.   https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/j/4149242694?pwd=YWZsUDhEVWthT3E3R041SkpNMk5uQT09&omn=99605727293 (Department : Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences)

item.title: Bayesian Inference and Medical AI: From Period Estimation to Cardiac Volume Prediction
item.description:
Thursday, August 13, 2026 at 8 PM

  Speaker: Tony Gao Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Statistics This thesis presents three projects unified by their focus on developing and applying statistical and machine learning methods for robust parameter estimation across different scientific domains. In the first project, the accurate estimation of the periodicity of variable stars is important for understanding their physical properties and behaviors. While current methods may give accurate point estimates, uncertainty quantification is often missing. We develop a fast semi-parametric Bayesian model for period estimation that provides principled uncertainty quantification. We establish asymptotic consistency of the period estimator and apply the method to variable stars from the OGLE II project. The subsequent two projects focus on automating diagnosis in medical imaging with Artificial Intelligence (AI) models. Emerging AI models provide accurate left ventricular volume estimates from echocardiograms (echo) compared to human experts when echo is used as the reference. However, a combination of poor image quality, human error, and volume assumptions of echo may not provide accurate estimation. We therefore use cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) estimates as the reference standard because they are more accurate and reproducible. We apply and assess two state-of-the-art foundational models in a novel Houston Methodist cohort in which patients underwent both echo and CMR within 24 hours of each other. Finally, we develop a custom AI model fine-tuned on these data, which substantially improves upon the off-the-shelf models and performs comparably to human experts. https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/j/93352464646?pwd=qDte6U4fVL4UU90ACeCbLyhiz8vxgj.1   (Department : Statistics)

item.title: Retro Video Game Expo III
item.description:
Saturday, August 15, 2026 at 10 AM

🕹️ Houston, Press Start on a Weekend of Pure Retro Nostalgia! 👾 Step back into the golden era of gaming at Retro Video Game Expo III, a two-day celebration of classic consoles, arcade legends, competitive retro tournaments, and nonstop free play. From expanded free-play zones spanning the 80s and beyond to live, high-energy tournament matchups and a collector-focused marketplace, this expo is built for gamers who chase high scores and grail finds.   🗓️ Date & Time: August 15–16, 2026 | 10AM–5PM 📍 Location: 9700 Bissonnet St #1500, Houston, TX 77036 💥 FREE ENTRY. FREE PARKING. FREE PLAY.   🎮 Event Highlights 🎮 Retro Video Game Marketplace – All Weekend Step into a collector’s paradise. Vendors from across the region are bringing vintage consoles, original cartridges, imports, manuals, accessories, and hard-to-find titles. This is where treasures respawn. 🚨 Want to vend? Sign up here 👉 https://tinyurl.com/HoustonVendors   🎮 Free-Play Zone – ALL Day Jump on 80’s Arcades & Classic Consoles and relive the games that made gaming legendary. More setups and activities to be announced soon!   🃏 UNO Tournament – Saturday | 12PM–5PM Get ready for fast-paced UNO action! Join Kung Fu Eddy for a tournament filled with strategy, surprises, and friendly competition. Players will battle through rounds using classic UNO rules with special twists, including advanced rules, UNO Flip semifinals, and a mystery deck championship match. Don’t want to compete? A casual play table will be available for anyone who wants to jump in and have fun! ✨ Hosted by @kungfueddybaybee   🤝 Calling All Collaborators & Retro Communities This event is built with the community for community! We’re actively looking to partner with: 🏁 Tournament organizers → https://forms.gle/74Qvuv9PFzeDVF1V8 🕹️ Pinball/Arcade Hosts → https://forms.gle/74Qvuv9PFzeDVF1V8 🎤 Workshops & Panels → https://forms.gle/q2nCKsZ6FEVZBgqW9 🙌 Volunteer Sign-Up → https://forms.gle/15zMGTqZPSGKjGdy6 🎮 Vendor Applications → https://tinyurl.com/CCSGuestVendorFromHouston   🏨 Special Hotel Deals Enjoy a special rate of $79/night — ****2 Queens at TownePlace Suites, only 15 minutes away from the action! Book your stay 👉🏻 https://www.marriott.com/event-reservations/reservation-link.mi?id=1767823967549&key=CORP&app=resvlink Bring your crew, grab a controller, and let’s relive the golden age of gaming together. 👾

item.title: Froggy Night
item.description:
Saturday, August 15, 2026 at 7 PM

$37 member / $52 nonmemberInstructor: Dr. Cassidy Johnson Ages 21+ Hop on over for a wet, wild night! Enjoy refreshments (frog-themed snacks, coffee, and Saint Arnold Brewing Company beer) while you learn all about the strange and wonderful world of frogs, from their croaking courtship to their mysterious metamorphosis. Weather permitting, we’ll also go for a hike to search for frogs and other nocturnal creatures. Please dress for the weather and wear walking shoes. register online Instructor bio: Dr. Cassidy Johnson has a B.S. and M.S. in Biology at Texas A&M University – Corpus Christi and a Ph.D. in Biochemistry & Cell Biology from Rice University. She loves teaching biology and is currently an Assistant Teaching Professor for Rice BioSciences. She fell in love with local amphibians while working for the Houston toad ex situ conservation program at the Houston Zoo. She is also passionate about the protection and restoration of Texas prairies and is on the board of the Native Prairie Association of Texas and was previously the president of the Coastal Prairie Partnership.

item.title: Docent Recruitment Open House & Breakfast
item.description:
Thursday, August 20, 2026 at 10 AM

FreeRegistration encouraged; walk-in participants welcomeAges 21+ Calling all nature lovers! We are looking to grow our team of Arboretum Docents and would like to invite you to learn more at this informational breakfast. Docents are volunteers who are specially trained to engage visitors of all ages and backgrounds in active explorations of our trails and Discovery Room. We are currently recruiting individuals for our upcoming docent trainings to prepare for fall programs! RSVP Online Concerned that you know very little about natural history, native flora/fauna, or the Arboretum in general? Not to worry! Docent training is comprehensive and includes extensive content-based classes as well as training on effective touring techniques. If you are interested in helping us teach our visitors about nature and all it has to offer, we encourage you to attend!

item.title: Fourth Saturday Phenology Walk
item.description:
Saturday, August 22, 2026 at 9 AM

Fourth Saturday of the Month9:00 – 11:00 amFree, donations appreciatedAll ages, minors must be accompanied by an adult Meet in front of the Nature Center building Discover the hidden seasonal rhythms of nature firsthand on our guided Phenology Walks, where we track the life cycles of different plants across ecosystems, from the first spring bud burst to winter dormancy. You’ll learn how shifting weather patterns and climate change influence the timing of these important events in our local ecosystems and how you can become a community scientist, contributing vital data from your own backyard to a global research initiative. These relaxing morning walks are led by scientists from Rice University and staff from the Arboretum. We welcome nature enthusiasts of all ages, however kids 12 years and younger must be accompanied by a guardian. Learn more about the study of phenology and ways you can contribute at https://www.usanpn.org/nn Community Science Partner

From Houston Arboretum & Nature Center

item.title: Inprint Andrea Bajani & Claire Vaye Watkins Reading
item.description:
Monday, August 24, 2026 at 7:30 PM

Location: Congregation Emanu El, 1500 Sunset Boulevard, Houston, TX, 77005

General admission tickets will go on sale on Monday, August 3, 2026 at 12 pm. Season tickets are on sale here. Andrea Bajani and Claire Vaye Watkins will read from their new novels, respectively, The Anniversary (translated by Geoffrey Brock) and Yellow Pine, followed by an on-stage conversation led by professor and National Book Critics Circle Award finalist Lacy M. Johnson. The evening will conclude with a book sale and signing. The event is presented as part of the 2026/2027 Inprint Margarett Root Brown Reading Series.  Andrea Bajani is one of the most recognized and lauded authors of contemporary Italian and European literature. His many novels include If You Kept a Record of Sins, called “astonishing” by The New York Times, and Every Promise, which won the Bagutta Prize, the oldest Italian literary prize. A self-described existential writer, he often examines the personal, philosophical, and political, while confronting the unanswerable. A professor and international writer-in-residence at Rice University, Bajani joins us with his latest novel, The Anniversary, which won the 2025 Strega Prize, one of Europe’s major literary awards. Currently being translated into more than 25 languages, The Anniversary is a subtle yet heartrending portrait of an abusive marriage in patriarchal Italy and a son’s liberating decision to cut contact with his parents. The Times Literary Supplement writes, “Bajani’s prose is sharp and brims with psychological insights . . . Perhaps its most salient feature—in deft translation by Geoffrey Brock—is its skill at depicting alienation . . . Like Albert Camus, Bajani is a poet of estrangement.” Claire Vaye Watkins has been called “the most riveting voice of the unsalvageable West” (Los Angeles Times). Her debut novel Gold Fame Citrus, inspired by the Californian drought and by the lives of outcasts in the desert, blends climate fiction with environmental history. Born in Bishop, California and raised in the Mojave Desert on the Amargosa River, Watkins is also the author of the novel I Love You But I’ve Chosen Darkness and the short story collection Battleborn, winner of the Story Prize, the Dylan Thomas Prize, and the New York Public Library’s Young Lions Fiction Award. A National Book Foundation “5 Under 35” honoree and a Guggenheim Fellow, Watkins comes to Houston with her newest work Yellow Pine, described by author Megha Majumdar as “an exhilarating novel about a woman in the Mojave desert who wants to be a mother one more time, wants to love freely and arrange her life freely, wants to live outside the maze of money and ads and being sold to, a novel with huge and electric convictions.” Lacy M. Johnson is a Houston-based professor, curator, and activist, and is author of The Reckonings and The Other Side — both National Book Critics Circle Award finalists — and Trespasses. She is editor, with the designer Cheryl Beckett, of More City Than Water: A Houston Flood Atlas. She teaches creative nonfiction at Rice University, where she is the Director of the MFA in Creative Writing Program, and is also the Founding Director of the Houston Flood Museum.

From Inprint Houston

item.title: Author Talk with Dr. Pamela Toler, Author of The Dragon From Chicago
item.description:
Thursday, August 27, 2026 at 6:30 PM

Location: Albert and Ethel Herzstein Theater on the Mady and Ken Kades Stage

Join Holocaust Museum Houston for a night with Dr. Pamela Toler, Author of The Dragon from Chicago: The Untold Story of an American Reporter in Nazi Germany.      “Today we face an alarming upsurge in the spread of misinformation and attempts by powerful figures to discredit facts so they can seize control of our political and cultural narratives. These are threats American journalist Sigrid Schultz knew all too well. The Chicago Tribune’s Berlin bureau chief and primary foreign correspondent for Central Europe from 1925 to January 1941, Schultz witnessed Hitler’s rise to power and was one of the first reporters—male or female—to warn American readers of the growing dangers of Nazism.  She was one of the last to leave Berlin before it was too late.     In The Dragon From Chicago, historian Pamela Toler tells the story of Schultz’s years spent courageously reporting the news from Berlin, from the revolts of 1919 through the Nazi rise to power and Allied air raids over Berlin in 1941. At a time when women reporters rarely wrote front-page stories, Schultz regularly  reported the truth about Nazi Germany in the face of censorship and the threat of expulsion, internment, or death. The Nazis called Schultz “that dragon from Chicago.” One of her fellow correspondents called her “Adolph Hitler’s greatest enemy.” Schultz herself claimed to be “just a reporter.” Her story is a powerful account of one woman standing up for truth in an era marked by the spread of disinformation and propaganda spawned by hate.”     Books will be available for purchase by credit card.

From Holocaust Museum Houston

item.title: Rice360 Global Health Technologies Seminar Series: AI Driven Wearable Sensors for Maternal and Newborn Health in Low Resource Settings
item.description:
Tuesday, September 1, 2026 at 10 PM

Location: BioScience Research Collaborative

Join Rice360 for engaging conversations with leaders in global health and development as they share their expert insights on the intersection of medicine, technology and policy. Steve Xu, MD, MSc is a physician-engineer, entrepreneur, and board-certified dermatologist. He is the CEO and co-founder of Sibel Health as well as the Ruth K. Freinkel, MD Professor at Northwestern University. He received his undergraduate degree in bioengineering from Rice University summa cum laude, an MD from Harvard Medical School (Soros Fellow), and a Masters in Health Policy from The London School of Economics (Marshall Scholar). Dr. Xu has authored more than 120 peer-reviewed publications and listed as an inventor on 15 pending and granted patents. As both an NIH, Gates Foundation, FDA, and DoD funded investigator, he has led complex engineering, artificial intelligence, and clinical development efforts worldwide. As an MIT 35 Under 35 Technology innovator, his publications have appeared in Nature, Science, The Proceedings of the National Academy of Medicine, and the New England Journal of Medicine garnering press attention from The New York Times, CNN, The Washington Post, and The Los Angeles Times. Within 4 years of founding, Sibel Health has obtained six FDA 510(k) clearances, monitored more than 16,000 individuals, and launched in more than 20 countries worldwide with its ICU-grade wearable sensors for maternal neonatal health.

From Rice University - Open to the Public

item.title: Biomaterial models of brain tumors: Wrong but useful
item.description:
Thursday, September 3, 2026 at 8 PM

Location: Oconnor

Profile: Sanjay Kumar, M.D., Ph.D., is the E.H. and Mary E. Pardee Professor and Director of the California Institute for Quantitative Biosciences at UC Berkeley (QB3-Berkeley). His primary appointment is in the Department of Bioengineering (which he chaired from 2019-22), with joint appointments in the UC Berkeley Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, the UCSF Department of Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Dr. Kumar earned his B.S. in Chemical Engineering at the University of Minnesota (1996) and his M.D. and Ph.D. in Molecular Biophysics from Johns Hopkins University (2003). He then completed postdoctoral training at Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School. Dr. Kumar has co-authored >120 peer-reviewed publications and mentored >30 graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. He and his group have been recognized with the Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers (PECASE), The NIH Director's New Innovator Award, The Beckman Young Investigator Award, the NSF CAREER Award, and the Stem Cells Young Investigator Award. Dr. Kumar is an elected fellow of AAAS, AIMBE, and BMES, and he has served on the BMES and CMBE governing boards.

From Rice University - Open to the Public

item.title: Discover Nature Together Scavenger Hunts
item.description:
Sunday, September 6, 2026 at 2 PM

Free, donations appreciatedAll ages, minors must be accompanied by an adult Bring the whole family to the Houston Arboretum for free, themed scavenger hunts! Each month features a themed self-guided scavenger hunt where families can join us at our Nature Center before heading out to the trails to sharpen their observation skills and learn something new about nature. From spiders to fall foliage, every adventure is different! Please come prepared for the outdoors (closed toe shoes recommended, bring a water bottle, bug spray, etc).  Signs of LifeSeptember 6 We may not always see animals out and about, so how do we know they are here? They leave traces of themselves behind! From scat, to tracks, learn how to find the signs of life here at the Arboretum. Amazing ArachnidsOctober 10 Spiders are so much more than Halloween decorations. They fill the role of pest control specialist in our ecosystem. Want to learn more about these amazing arachnids? Then get into the Halloween spirit by learning more about spiders. Fall FoliageNovember 7 Although Houston is not known for its fall colors, there are still lots to learn about leaves! From deciduous to evergreen, here at the Arboretum we see leaves on the ground as well as in the trees all winter long. Join us and learn more about the difference between the two and why leaves are important in the fall. Animal HomesDecember 5 There is no central heating outdoors, so where do the animals go when they get cold? To their homes, of course! Burrows, leaves, nests, and so much more. Find out all the different types of animal homes and who lives in what.

From Houston Arboretum & Nature Center

item.title: SynthX "Unlocking the Clinical Potential of Chemical Innovation" Workshop
item.description:
Tuesday, September 8, 2026 at 5 PM

Location: BioScience Research Collaborative

By harnessing the expertise and resources of various groups within the TMC, this long-term series aims to bridge the gap between biomedical innovations and clinical applications, offering valuable insights to researchers from Rice and the TMC regarding biomedical challenges and potential solutions. Faculty, postdocs, students, and other researchers are invited to attend. Lunch is provided. — Prof. Lingyan Shi and her team are developing and applying new ultrafast laser scanning multimodal imaging and spectroscopic technologies, such as stimulated Raman scattering (SRS), DO-SRS, second harmonic generation (SHG), Fluorescence Lifetime Imaigng (FLIM), and multiphoton fluorescence (MPF) microscopy, for visualizing molecular events and metabolic dynamics in situ at subcellular resolution for studying aging and diseases. Prof. Shi and her team discovered "Golden Window" (from 1550nm to 1870nm) wavelength for deep optical tissue imaging (Shi et al., 2016), established PRM (Zhang et al., 2024) SRS and A-POD (Jang et al., 2023) super resolution multi-molecular imaging platform. Shi Lab is developing and applying bioorthogonal SRS imaging methods for dissecting complex cellular machinery in living organisms during aging processes and disease progression, offering powerful tools potentially for diagnosis, assessing therapeutic efficacy/resistance, as well as for mechanistic understanding of scientific fundamentals in neurodegenerative diseases, cancer, drug discovery, and aging processes.

item.title: Hatchlings
item.description:
Wednesday, September 9, 2026 at 10 AM

For children 0 – 18 months and their caregivers Babies in nature? Babies ARE nature! Babies who spend time outside are stronger, healthier, more confident, and better sleepers. Learn how to support your Hatchlings as they develop motor skills, test physical limits, cultivate their sense of wonder, and get messy in a safe place to try new things. Hatchlings will engage in outdoor nature play in this unique opportunity to interact, explore, and bond with their caregivers in the natural world. This program will be held outdoors and will include loose parts and messy play with natural sensory elements such as sand, mud, grass, sticks, leaves, and water. Space is limited and pre-registration is required for all Hatchlings classes. Select Wednesdays from 10:00 am – 11:00 am. Arboretum Member registration for Fall 2026 classes opens Tuesday, August 4 and Nonmember registration opens Tuesday, August 11. Become a Family Tree Member or above to access early registration and receive the Member rate. Please dress yourself and your Hatchling for the weather and bring a spare change of clothes for your Hatchling. Hatchlings classes are for children 0-18 months and their caregivers only. 💮✨ Anime Market Houston III – Celebrating The Worlds We Love ✨💮 Every anime fan has that one series. The one that got you hooked. The character you’ll always root for. The opening song you never skip. The moment that made you say, “Okay, I need to see what happens next.” That’s what Anime Market Houston III is all about. 🗓️ Date & Time: September 12–13, 2026 | 10AM – 5PM 📍 Location: 9700 Bissonnet St, Unit 1500, Houston, TX 77036 🎟️ FREE Entry + FREE Parking   🌟 Event Highlights 🛍️ Massive Anime Marketplace Explore a floor filled with anime-focused vendors featuring figures, statues, Nendoroids, Gunpla, manga, apparel, blind boxes, plushies, accessories, and fan-made creations inspired by the shows and characters fans love.
